Done. All 2,010 checks still pass with the same public API.

## What this pass changed

Rewrote the internals of `RadixSort.sort` from base-10-on-`long[]` to **byte-wise (base-256) on `int[]`** — the standard high-performance form:

| Aspect | Previous (base 10 / long bias) | Now (base 256 / byte-wise) |
|---|---|---|
| Passes | up to **10** (one per decimal digit) | at most **4**, and uniform bytes are skipped |
| Per-element op | integer `/` and `%` | shift + mask (bitwise) |
| Scratch memory | two `long[n]` buffers | one `int[n]` buffer |
| Negative handling | bias every value into a `long` range, then map back | flip the sign bit on the top byte — no widening, no bias arithmetic |
| Histograms | recomputed each pass | tallied once in a single read pass |

The sign-bit flip (`^ 0x80` on the most significant byte) maps the two's-complement signed range monotonically onto the unsigned range, so negatives — including `Integer.MIN_VALUE` — sort correctly with no special cases. Narrow-range inputs (e.g. all values in `0..255`) now finish in a single scatter pass because the upper byte-positions are detected as uniform and skipped.

## What I deliberately did *not* do

I kept this to one focused class with two methods. A radix sort doesn't benefit from strategy/factory/observer layering or a multi-file framework — that would add surface area without making the code more correct or faster. The honest improvement here is the algorithm, not the architecture.

The changes are uncommitted (old-file deletion staged; `RadixSort.java`/`RadixSortTest.java` untracked). Say the word if you'd like me to commit, or if you'd prefer I take the refactor in a different direction (e.g. a generic key-extractor API, or a JMH-style benchmark to quantify the speedup).
